evals.prompt: Define usability testing in 2-3 sentences. Name its core method and what it produces.
expected_elements: Watching real people attempt realistic tasks on a prototype or product to surface obstacles
It is empirical observation, not expert opinion or prediction
Core method is the think-aloud protocol (Ericsson & Simon); organized around task scenarios and a neutral moderator
Produces severity-rated usability findings the team can triage

evals.prompt: Why is direct observation necessary — why can't designers and engineers just predict where users will struggle?
expected_elements: The mental models that make a design feel obvious to its creators are exactly the models a fresh user lacks
Only direct observation closes that gap
The discipline replaces 'I think users will understand' with 'we watched users; here is what happened'
A session that confirms the design entirely is suspect (tasks too easy or moderator helping)

evals.prompt: Contrast moderated and unmoderated usability testing. What does each gain and give up?
expected_elements: Moderated: richer data, ability to follow up on surprises; higher cost, requires scheduling
Unmoderated: lower cost, scales to dozens of sessions; sacrifices follow-up on surprises
Choice depends on whether probing unexpected behavior or volume/cost matters more

evals.prompt: A PM asks how many participants are needed to test an onboarding prototype. What do you tell them, and what caveats apply?
expected_elements: ~5 users (Nielsen/Landauer 5-user rule) surfaces ~85% of major problems with diminishing returns after
Applies per homogeneous user segment and per discrete task scope
Applies to formative (diagnostic, iterative) testing only
Summative/benchmark claims need much larger samples — do not apply the 5-user rule to them

evals.prompt: How should task scenarios be written for a usability test, and how should findings be organized afterward?
expected_elements: Write tasks as goals, not step-by-step instructions ('find out how much you owe' not 'click the Tax tab')
A participant could complete the task without being shown the design first
Organize findings by Nielsen's 0-4 severity scale (cosmetic / minor / major / catastrophic)
Optionally complement with quantitative measures (task success rate, time on task, SUS)

evals.prompt: An engineer asks you to 'set up usability testing' meaning unit and integration tests in CI. Is that this skill? Why or why not?
expected_elements: No — that is testing-strategy (automated verification of code correctness)
Usability testing is empirical observation of real humans attempting tasks
The shared word 'test' hides two unrelated activities
Correctly redirects engineering verification to testing-strategy

evals.prompt: A stakeholder argues '5 users is enough to prove our redesign improved success rate by 12%.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: The 5-user rule is for formative diagnostic testing, not summative/statistical claims
A success-rate comparison is a summative/benchmark claim needing a much larger sample
5 users surfaces ~85% of major problems per segment/task — it does not establish statistical significance
Conflating formative and summative purposes is a classic, invalidating error

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a usability test was run well and its findings are trustworthy?
expected_elements: Tasks are goals, not instructions; a participant could complete them without seeing the design first
Moderator script has no leading prompts or defensive explanations; most common utterances are 'what are you thinking?' and silence
Findings are severity-rated, not just listed flat
Sample size matches the claim type (5 for formative; justified separately for summative)
At least one finding contradicts a designer/PM expectation; recordings/notes preserve specific behavior
